mcqs.question: A product catalog page is read 100,000 times a day and its underlying data is updated only a handful of times a day. Why is this a strong candidate for denormalization?
options: The read-to-write ratio is extremely high, so a small, infrequent write cost avoids paying a join cost on every one of the 100,000 daily reads
Denormalization is always beneficial regardless of read/write ratio
Product catalogs can never be modeled with normalized tables in the first place
It reduces the total number of rows stored in the database
mcqs.explanation: The decision should follow the actual read-to-write ratio: a high ratio means the aggregate savings on reads vastly outweigh the rare write-time sync cost. Denormalization is a trade-off, not a universal win; product catalogs are perfectly normalizable; and denormalization typically adds redundant storage, it doesn't reduce it.

mcqs.question: An order_items row stores product_name as it was at the time of purchase, separate from the live products.name column, which can later change. What's the actual benefit here?
options: It reduces the number of tables in the schema
It captures a point-in-time snapshot, so historical orders correctly show the name at purchase time even after the product is later renamed
It removes the need for a products table entirely
It automatically prevents the product from ever being renamed
mcqs.explanation: This denormalization is actually more correct than a live join in this case — a historical record should reflect what was true at the time, not the current live value. It doesn't reduce table count, doesn't eliminate the need for a products table, and doesn't restrict renaming — it just decouples history from a live value that can still change.

mcqs.question: Why do most systems keep their transactional orders/payments tables normalized while building a separate denormalized reporting/analytics table?
options: Normalized and denormalized schemas cannot coexist in the same organization
Reporting queries are illegal to run against a normalized schema
It isolates small, correctness-critical transactional writes from large, read-heavy analytical queries, so neither workload's needs compromise the other's schema
Denormalized tables are always smaller in total storage than normalized ones
mcqs.explanation: Separating the two workloads means the transactional system stays optimized for fast, correct small writes, while the analytics side is optimized for read-heavy queries without either compromising the other. Both schema styles coexist constantly in real systems; reporting queries against normalized data are entirely legal, just slower; denormalized tables usually use MORE total storage due to redundancy.

mcqs.question: A team denormalizes order_count onto the customers table but never sets up any trigger, application-level update, or reconciliation job to maintain it. What happens over time?
options: The value silently drifts from the true count whenever any write path doesn't explicitly update it, with nothing flagging the discrepancy
The database automatically recalculates it whenever it's queried
PostgreSQL and MySQL both refuse to allow denormalized columns without a trigger
The column will always stay correct as long as the primary key doesn't change
mcqs.explanation: A denormalized column is just a plain column — nothing keeps it accurate unless an explicit mechanism (trigger, application code, or reconciliation job) is wired up, so any missed write path causes silent drift. Databases don't auto-recompute denormalized values on read, don't block their creation, and primary key stability has nothing to do with keeping a separate cached column correct.

mcqs.question: A team denormalizes reporting columns directly onto the live orders table to speed up a dashboard. What's the main risk to the checkout flow?
options: The checkout flow becomes completely unable to insert new orders
Every transactional write to orders now also has to maintain the reporting columns, adding latency and coupling risk to the exact path that most needs to stay fast and simple
SQL no longer allows inserting into a table with more than a certain number of columns
The orders table can no longer have a primary key once reporting columns are added
mcqs.explanation: Coupling analytical and transactional concerns onto the same table means every checkout write also pays the cost of maintaining reporting data, and a reporting-driven schema change now risks breaking the checkout path. There's no such insert-blocking failure, no SQL column-count restriction relevant here, and adding columns doesn't affect the primary key.
